fields.v: Jiang, Z., Wang, R., Hu, Y., Wang, Y., Jia, Y., Gong, N. Z. (2026). Self-Evolving Coding Rules for AI Coding Agents. arXiv:2610.00650v1 [cs.CL], 30 Sep 2026
Preprint (arXiv); page 1 footer reads '40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)', suggesting a conference paper (acceptance to be confirmed)
Duke University (all six authors)

Proposes an approach (RuleEvolve, self-evolving framework for coding rules / AGENTS.md); secondary: compares (vs no rule, manual rule, Prompt-Ops, across 2 agent frameworks, 4 models, 3 benchmarks + SWE-bench Lite)

RuleEvolve (no version): pool of m candidate coding rules evolved by an LLM mutator and a judge module, with strategic mutation allocation based on Optimal Computing Budget Allocation (OCBA). Baselines: No rule; Manual rule (from awesome-cursorrules repository, App. F); Prompt-Ops (LLM prompt duel optimizer, default settings); ablations: even and proportional allocation

Coding rules file (AGENTS.md for OpenHands; system prompt for OpenAI SDK agent). Evolved rule has 16 sections in six categories (output format/self-containment, algorithm knowledge, brevity style, API/library idiom, correctness tactics, process/budget)

Initial rules -> mutator generates m variants -> judge runs agent on mini-batch of training tasks and scores (code characters + lambda x correctness penalty vs no-rule) -> allocate N mutations by OCBA -> evaluate -> prune to top m -> repeat T iterations -> return best rule
None (automatic loop); only the initial rule is human-written
Single artefact (coding rules / context file), evolved and then used by the agent
Not classifiable (coding rules / AGENTS.md, no specification)
Mostly function-level code generation from a problem description (BigCodeBench, BigCodeBench-Hard, HumanEval); existing code base only in SWE-Bench Lite (repository-level issues)

Training: 1,000 random BigCodeBench instances (mini-batches of B = 10); testing: 100 random samples each of BCB (disjoint), BCB-Hard, HumanEval; SWE-Bench Lite 100-task subset. Parameters T = 10, N = 20, m = 5, lambda = 3,000
Python programming tasks (general, library function calls); SWE-Bench Lite Python repositories
N/A (no human participants)

Tasks: 100-sample test sets of BCB, BCB-Hard, HumanEval; SWE-Bench Lite 100 tasks. Configurations: 4 methods x 2 frameworks (OpenAI SDK custom agent, OpenHands) x 4 backbones; rules evolved per model. Baselines: No rule, Manual rule, Prompt-Ops; ablation: even/proportional allocation, T, N, m. Held constant: framework, backbone, test samples within comparison. Acceptance tests: benchmark test cases. Repetitions: single run per cell in main tables; 10 seeds for one configuration. Human intervention: none. Mutator LLM not stated

RuleEvolve reaches highest or near-highest PR and lower code length/tokens than No rule and Manual rule in most cells, e.g. OpenAI SDK gpt-5.3-codex BCB PR 0.49 vs 0.45 manual, chars 453.1 vs 2372, tokens 544.5 vs 1022; gpt-5-mini BCB 0.46 vs 0.31 manual, ~40% fewer tokens. Prompt-Ops sometimes cheaper but drops PR (OpenHands BCB 0.43 vs 0.52). Multi-seed: PR equal (0.502) with fewer lines (24.3 vs 32.5) and tokens (1019 vs 1181). SWE-Bench Lite: 0.340 vs 0.330 no rule, with time 297 s vs 131 s. App. D: lower cyclomatic complexity (5.37 -> 3.95) and Halstead volume, maintainability index 78.3 vs 85.1, docstring rate 47% -> 1%. No significance tests

Distinguished methods mainly on length and tokens; PR differences small (often 0.01-0.03 on 100 samples). Repeatability: 10-seed check for one configuration only (SDs 0.015-0.032 on PR, comparable to differences). Limitations stated: brevity objective may slightly lower PR on complex tasks; stochasticity and bias of LLM mutator/judge; length used as proxy for cost; maintainability and architecture not explored

Coding rules can be evolved to cut code length and inference cost while keeping correctness. Limitations: possible PR drop on complex tasks; mutator/judge stochasticity and bias; other dimensions (maintainability, architectural complexity) left to future work
